pucopd1.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd1.q: Which regular therapy is acceptable on its own in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease but never on its own in asthma?
opts: An inhaled corticosteroid
In asthma the inhaled corticosteroid is the mainstay controller; in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease a steroid is added only at the top group, combined, when asthma features overlap.
reversed direction or value
A leukotriene receptor antagonist
A leukotriene receptor antagonist is an other controller option in asthma and is not on the chronic obstructive pulmonary disease table; long-acting bronchodilators are.
adjacent fact
An anti-immunoglobulin E antibody
Omalizumab is an asthma add-on for the top step; the chronic obstructive pulmonary disease groups list bronchodilators and no biologics.
adjacent fact
A long-acting beta-2 agonist

Correct. In chronic obstructive pulmonary disease a long-acting muscarinic antagonist or a long-acting beta-2 agonist alone is regular treatment; in asthma a long-acting beta-2 agonist is never used alone.

pucopd1.io: Outline appropriate patient education for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd1.q: In which form is nicotine polacrilex given?
opts: Patch
The patch is the nicotine transdermal system; nicotine polacrilex is the gum.
adjacent fact
Spray
The nicotine spray is a separate listed form; nicotine polacrilex is the gum.
adjacent fact
Inhaler
The nicotine inhaler is a separate listed form; nicotine polacrilex is the gum.
adjacent fact
Gum
Correct. Nicotine polacrilex is the nicotine gum; with the patches, the gum is available over the counter.

pucopd1.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd1.q: For which patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is long-term oxygen therapy listed?
opts: Those with persistent hypoxemia
Correct. Long-term oxygen therapy is listed, for patients in any group, if there is chronic (persistent) hypoxemia.
Those in the high-risk groups
High risk (two or more exacerbations a year) moves a patient to group C or D and decides the inhaler, not oxygen; oxygen is listed for chronic hypoxemia.
adjacent fact
Those with asthma overlap
Features of asthma overlap make a combination glucocorticoid-long-acting beta-2 agonist inhaler preferred in group D; long-term oxygen is for chronic hypoxemia.
adjacent fact
Those who still smoke
Smokers are told to avoid the risk factor and are offered cessation; long-term oxygen therapy is listed for chronic hypoxemia.
common lay belief

pucopd1.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd1.q: In chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, when do symptoms generally develop?
opts: Before lung function begins to decline
Lung function falls first; patients stay asymptomatic while it is normal and early in its decline, and symptoms appear after a significant fall in forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1).
reversed direction or value
After a significant decline in lung function
Correct. Symptoms generally develop only after a significant decline in forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) has occurred, and they progress as lung function deteriorates further.
As soon as lung function first falls
Patients remain asymptomatic in the first stretch of reduced lung function; symptoms develop only after a significant decline in forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1).
wrong stage or severity
When lung function returns to normal
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is generally not fully reversible, and symptoms rise as forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) keeps falling after a significant decline.
reversed direction or value

pucopd1.io: Outline appropriate patient education for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd1.q: In a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, what can stopping smoking do to the decline in ventilatory function?
opts: Return it to the normal age-related rate
Correct. Smoking cessation can return the decline in ventilatory function to the normal age-related rate and reduce the risk of lung cancer.
Reverse the existing obstruction fully
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is generally not fully reversible; stopping smoking returns the rate of decline to the normal age-related rate.
common lay belief
Stop age-related decline entirely
Age-related decline continues after quitting; what cessation can do is return the decline to the normal age-related rate.
reversed direction or value
Speed it up for the first year
Quitting does not accelerate the decline; it can return the decline in ventilatory function to the normal age-related rate and reduce lung cancer risk.
reversed direction or value

pucopd1.io: Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of respiratory drugs
pucopd1.q: Which black box warning is listed for varenicline?
opts: Lowered seizure threshold
A seizure disorder is the reason bupropion is avoided; varenicline's black box warning is for neuropsychiatric events.
adjacent fact
Cardiac tachyarrhythmias
Tachyarrhythmias are the cardiovascular caution for nicotine replacement; varenicline's black box warning is for neuropsychiatric events.
adjacent fact
Neuropsychiatric events
Correct. Varenicline's black box warning is for neuropsychiatric events such as depression and suicidal ideation.
Severe liver toxicity
Hepatitis is a concern with isoniazid and pyrazinamide; varenicline's black box warning is for neuropsychiatric events such as depression and suicidal ideation.
adjacent fact

pucopd1.io: Describe the molecular mechanism of action of drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd1.q: How is bupropion thought to help a smoker quit?
opts: It partially stimulates nicotine receptors
Partial nicotine receptor agonism, to a lesser degree than nicotine, is varenicline's mechanism; bupropion inhibits norepinephrine and dopamine uptake.
confused mechanism or drug class
It replaces nicotine to ease withdrawal
Replacing nicotine to reduce craving and withdrawal is what the patch, gum, spray and inhaler do; bupropion inhibits norepinephrine and dopamine uptake.
confused mechanism or drug class
It inhibits norepinephrine and dopamine uptake

Correct. Nicotine indirectly activates epinephrine and dopamine in the central nervous system, and bupropion is postulated to mimic these effects because it inhibits the uptake of norepinephrine and dopamine.
It blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors
Blocking acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors is the anticholinergic bronchodilator mechanism; bupropion inhibits norepinephrine and dopamine uptake.
confused mechanism or drug class

pucopd1.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd1.q: What determines the dose and duration of nicotine replacement therapy?
opts: Body weight and kidney function
Renal function guides many drug adjustments, but nicotine replacement is set by the patient's level of dependence and point in therapy.
adjacent fact
The age at which smoking began
The age smoking began is not what sets therapy; nicotine replacement depends on the level of dependence and the point in therapy.
common lay belief
The number of past quit attempts
Past quit attempts are not the stated basis; the dose and duration depend on the level of dependence and the point in therapy.
common lay belief
Dependence level and stage of treatment
Correct. The dose and duration of nicotine replacement depend on the patient's level of dependence and point in therapy; the duration is between 6 and 12 weeks.

pucopd1.io: Describe the molecular mechanism of action of drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd1.q: Which smoking cessation agent is a partial nicotine receptor agonist?
opts: Bupropion
Bupropion is postulated to work by inhibiting norepinephrine and dopamine uptake; the partial nicotine receptor agonist is varenicline.
confused mechanism or drug class
Nicotine polacrilex
Nicotine polacrilex (gum) supplies nicotine itself to reduce craving and withdrawal; the partial agonist, acting to a lesser degree than nicotine, is varenicline.
confused mechanism or drug class
Nicotine transdermal system
The nicotine patch supplies nicotine itself to reduce craving and withdrawal; the partial nicotine receptor agonist is varenicline.
confused mechanism or drug class
Varenicline
Correct. Varenicline (Chantix) is a partial nicotine receptor agonist, acting to a lesser degree than nicotine.

pucopd1.io: Identify contraindications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd1.q: Nicotine replacement calls for caution in which patients?
opts: Those with cardiovascular problems
Correct. Nicotine replacement calls for caution in patients with cardiovascular problems because of the chance of tachyarrhythmias and hypertension.
Those with a seizure disorder
A seizure disorder is the reason to avoid bupropion; nicotine replacement calls for caution in cardiovascular problems.
adjacent fact
Those taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor
Monoamine oxidase inhibitors are a reason to avoid bupropion; nicotine replacement calls for caution in cardiovascular problems.
adjacent fact
Those with a history of depression
Depression and suicidal ideation are varenicline's boxed neuropsychiatric warning; nicotine replacement calls for caution in cardiovascular problems.
adjacent fact

pucopd1.io: Outline appropriate patient education for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd1.q: Which nicotine replacement forms are available over the counter?
opts: Spray and inhaler
The nicotine spray and inhaler are listed forms, but the ones named as over the counter are the patches and gum.
reversed direction or value
Patches and gum
Correct. Nicotine patches and gum are available over the counter; the spray and the inhaler are the other listed nicotine forms.
Gum and spray
The gum is over the counter, but the spray is not among the forms named as over the counter; those are the patches and gum.
adjacent fact
Patches and inhaler
The patches are over the counter, but the inhaler is not among the forms named as over the counter; those are the patches and gum.
adjacent fact

pucopd1.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd1.q: A high-risk patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has severe breathlessness and no features of asthma. What is the suggested regular treatment?
opts: A long-acting muscarinic antagonist alone
A long-acting muscarinic antagonist alone is the group D start when breathlessness is not severe, and the group C treatment; severe breathlessness calls for the combination.
wrong stage or severity
A short-acting bronchodilator as needed
As-needed short-acting bronchodilator alone is the group A treatment; a high-risk, severely breathless patient is group D.
wrong stage or severity
A long-acting beta-2 agonist plus muscarinic antagonist

Correct. Group D (more symptomatic, high risk) gets a long-acting muscarinic antagonist or, if breathlessness is severe, the combination of a long-acting beta-2 agonist and a long-acting muscarinic antagonist.
An inhaled glucocorticoid with a long-acting beta-2 agonist
The glucocorticoid-long-acting beta-2 agonist inhaler may be preferred only when features of asthma overlap, which this patient does not have.
ruled out by a stated finding

pucopd1.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd1.q: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease must stop to catch breath when walking on level ground and had one exacerbation last year without hospitalization. What is the suggested regular treatment?
opts: A short-acting bronchodilator as needed alone
As-needed short-acting bronchodilator alone is group A, the less symptomatic patient; stopping to catch breath on level ground makes this group B, which needs a regular long-acting bronchodilator.
wrong stage or severity
A long-acting muscarinic antagonist or beta-2 agonist

Correct. Group B (more symptomatic, low risk) gets regular treatment with one long-acting bronchodilator, either a muscarinic antagonist or a beta-2 agonist by patient preference, plus a short-acting bronchodilator as needed.
An inhaled glucocorticoid with a long-acting beta-2 agonist
A glucocorticoid-long-acting beta-2 agonist inhaler is considered in group D when asthma features overlap; this low-risk patient is group B.
wrong stage or severity
A long-acting beta-2 agonist plus muscarinic antagonist
The two long-acting bronchodilators together are for group D with severe breathlessness; with only one exacerbation and no hospitalization this patient is group B.
ruled out by a stated finding

pucopd1.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd1.q: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has frequent hospitalized exacerbations, marked breathlessness and features that overlap with asthma. Which inhaler may be preferred?
opts: A long-acting beta-2 agonist on its own
A long-acting beta-2 agonist is not used alone in asthma, and asthma overlap is the reason a glucocorticoid-long-acting beta-2 agonist combination may be preferred.
ruled out by a stated finding
A long-acting muscarinic antagonist on its own
A long-acting muscarinic antagonist alone is the group C and milder group D treatment; asthma overlap makes the glucocorticoid-long-acting beta-2 agonist inhaler preferable.
wrong stage or severity
A glucocorticoid plus long-acting beta-2 agonist
Correct. In group D a combination glucocorticoid-long-acting beta-2 agonist inhaler may be preferred if features of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease overlap.
A short-acting beta-2 agonist plus antimuscarinic
The short-acting beta-2 agonist and antimuscarinic combination is an as-needed group A choice; overlap with asthma in group D favors the glucocorticoid-long-acting beta-2 agonist inhaler.
wrong stage or severity

pucopd2.io: Outline appropriate patient education for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd2.q: Which factor directly correlates with a patient's success in quitting smoking?
opts: Using medication without counseling
Effective programs combine drug therapy with counseling rather than replacing it; the intensity and frequency of counseling correlate with success.
reversed direction or value
Daily cigarette count at the start
The level of dependence guides the dose and duration of nicotine replacement, but the factor tied directly to quitting success is the intensity and frequency of counseling.
adjacent fact
Length of the smoking history
Quitting is a complex physical, psychological and social issue; the factor that directly correlates with success is the intensity and frequency of counseling.
common lay belief
Intensity and frequency of counseling
Correct. Effective programs combine pharmacologic intervention with counseling, and the intensity and frequency of counseling directly correlate with the success of quitting.

pucopd2.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd2.q: What is the purpose of the nicotine replacement agents?
opts: To reduce craving and physical withdrawal
Correct. Nicotine replacement reduces the craving to smoke and minimizes physical withdrawal (anxiety, irritability, restlessness, insomnia, headache, depression and nausea).
To inhibit norepinephrine and dopamine uptake
Inhibiting norepinephrine and dopamine uptake is bupropion's postulated mechanism; nicotine replacement reduces craving and physical withdrawal.
confused mechanism or drug class
To partly block the nicotine receptor
Varenicline is the partial nicotine receptor agonist; nicotine replacement supplies nicotine to reduce craving and physical withdrawal.
confused mechanism or drug class
To make cigarettes taste unpleasant
Nicotine replacement does not work by aversion; it reduces the craving to smoke and minimizes physical withdrawal symptoms.
common lay belief

pucopd2.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd2.q: Why is annual influenza vaccination highly recommended for patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: Influenza triggers most asthma attacks
Viral respiratory infection triggers most asthma attacks, but the reason for the vaccine in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is the risk of serious influenza pneumonia.
adjacent fact
The vaccine slows the fall in lung function
Smoking cessation is what can return the decline in lung function to the normal rate; the vaccine guards against serious influenza pneumonia.
adjacent fact
It replaces the pneumococcal vaccine
Patients should also receive the pneumococcal vaccine; annual influenza vaccination is given because influenza pneumonia carries significant morbidity and mortality.
reversed direction or value
They risk serious pneumonia from influenza
Correct. Patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease are at risk for significant morbidity and mortality from pneumonia caused by influenza, so annual vaccination is highly recommended.

pucopd2.io: Identify contraindications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd2.q: A patient with a seizure disorder asks for help to stop smoking. Which agent should be avoided?
opts: Varenicline
Varenicline's listed side effects are nausea, sleep disturbance and headache, with a black box warning for neuropsychiatric events; the agent to avoid in a seizure disorder is bupropion.
adjacent fact
Bupropion
Correct. Bupropion sustained release is to be avoided in patients with seizure disorders and in patients taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors.
Nicotine gum
Nicotine replacement calls for caution in cardiovascular problems (tachyarrhythmias, hypertension); the agent to avoid in a seizure disorder is bupropion.
adjacent fact
Nicotine patch
The patch reduces craving and withdrawal and needs caution in cardiovascular problems; bupropion is the agent avoided in seizure disorders.
adjacent fact

pucopd2.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd2.q: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has mild symptoms but had two exacerbations last year, one needing hospitalization. What is the suggested regular treatment?
opts: A regular long-acting beta-2 agonist
A long-acting beta-2 agonist is one of the two group B choices; group C, the high-risk patient with mild symptoms, gets a long-acting muscarinic antagonist.
confused mechanism or drug class
A short-acting bronchodilator as needed
As-needed short-acting bronchodilator alone is for group A, the low-risk patient; two exacerbations with a hospitalization make this patient high risk, group C.
ruled out by a stated finding
A regular long-acting muscarinic antagonist

Correct. Group C (less symptomatic, high risk: two or more exacerbations a year with one or more hospitalized) gets regular treatment with a long-acting muscarinic antagonist, with a short-acting beta-2 agonist for relief.
An inhaled glucocorticoid with a long-acting beta-2 agonist
A glucocorticoid-long-acting beta-2 agonist inhaler is considered in group D when asthma features overlap; group C gets a long-acting muscarinic antagonist.
wrong stage or severity

pucopd2.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd2.q: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is breathless only with strenuous exercise and had no exacerbations last year. What is the suggested treatment?
opts: A short-acting bronchodilator as needed
Correct. Group A (mild or infrequent symptoms, 0 or 1 exacerbation without hospitalization) is treated with a short-acting bronchodilator, beta-2 agonist, antimuscarinic or both, as needed.
A regular long-acting bronchodilator
A regular long-acting bronchodilator is for group B, the more symptomatic low-risk patient; mild symptoms with no exacerbations is group A, a short-acting bronchodilator as needed.
wrong stage or severity
A regular long-acting muscarinic antagonist
A regular long-acting muscarinic antagonist is an option for groups B, C and D; this low-risk, mildly symptomatic patient is group A, which needs only a short-acting bronchodilator as needed.
wrong stage or severity
A long-acting beta-2 agonist plus muscarinic antagonist
The long-acting combination is reserved for group D with severe breathlessness; this patient is group A and needs only a short-acting bronchodilator as needed.
wrong stage or severity

pucopd2.io: Identify respiratory drug classes and commonly prescribed drugs for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd2.q: Which smoking cessation agent is marketed as Zyban?
opts: Varenicline
Varenicline is marketed as Chantix, a partial nicotine receptor agonist; Zyban is bupropion sustained release.
adjacent fact
Nicotine polacrilex
Nicotine polacrilex is the nicotine gum, available over the counter; Zyban is bupropion sustained release.
adjacent fact
Bupropion
Correct. Bupropion sustained release (Zyban) is one of the six listed smoking cessation agents, with the nicotine patch, gum, spray and inhaler, and varenicline (Chantix).
Nicotine transdermal system
The nicotine transdermal system is the patch, available over the counter; Zyban is bupropion sustained release.
adjacent fact

pucopd2.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd2.q: Which finding places a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in a high-risk treatment group?
opts: Two exacerbations a year, one hospitalized
Correct. High risk (groups C and D) is two or more exacerbations per year with one or more leading to hospitalization; 0 or 1 exacerbation without hospitalization is low risk.
Breathlessness walking on level ground
Breathlessness on level ground is the symptom axis, which separates more symptomatic (B, D) from less symptomatic (A, C) patients; risk is set by exacerbations.
competing diagnosis
Chronic hypoxemia needing oxygen
Chronic hypoxemia calls for long-term oxygen therapy in any group; the high-risk groups are defined by two or more exacerbations a year with a hospitalization.
adjacent fact
One exacerbation without hospitalization
Zero or one exacerbation in the past year without hospitalization is the low-risk definition (groups A and B); high risk needs two or more with a hospitalization.
wrong stage or severity

pucopd2.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd2.q: What is the usual duration of nicotine replacement therapy?
opts: 2 to 4 weeks
Two to four weeks is shorter than the stated course; nicotine replacement runs between 6 and 12 weeks.
reversed direction or value
6 to 12 weeks
Correct. The duration of nicotine replacement therapy is between 6 and 12 weeks, set by the level of dependence and point in therapy.
16 to 20 weeks
Sixteen to twenty weeks is longer than the stated course; nicotine replacement runs between 6 and 12 weeks.
reversed direction or value
24 to 52 weeks
Six months to a year is far longer than the stated course; nicotine replacement runs between 6 and 12 weeks.
reversed direction or value

pucopd2.io: Describe adverse effects of drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd2.q: Which side effects are listed for varenicline?
opts: Nausea, sleep disturbance and headache
Correct. Varenicline's listed side effects are nausea, sleep disturbance and headache, and it carries a black box warning for neuropsychiatric events.
Tachyarrhythmias and hypertension
Tachyarrhythmias and hypertension are the reason for caution with nicotine replacement in cardiovascular problems; varenicline causes nausea, sleep disturbance and headache.
adjacent fact
Orange tears, sweat and urine
Orange-colored secretions are a rifampin effect; varenicline's listed side effects are nausea, sleep disturbance and headache.
adjacent fact
Oral thrush and growth delay
Oral candidiasis and growth suppression in children belong to inhaled corticosteroids; varenicline causes nausea, sleep disturbance and headache.
adjacent fact

pucopd2.io: List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd2.q: Which measure is recommended for every patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, whatever the treatment group?
opts: A regular long-acting bronchodilator
A regular long-acting bronchodilator is the treatment for group B (and the long-acting muscarinic antagonist for groups C and D), not a measure for every patient; pneumococcal vaccination is.
wrong stage or severity
An inhaled glucocorticoid
A combination glucocorticoid-long-acting beta-2 agonist inhaler is considered in group D when asthma features overlap; pneumococcal vaccination applies to every group.
wrong stage or severity
A long-acting muscarinic antagonist
A regular long-acting muscarinic antagonist is the treatment for groups C and D; the measure for every group is pneumococcal vaccination, with annual influenza vaccination.
wrong stage or severity
Pneumococcal vaccination

Correct. Measures for all groups are avoiding risk factors such as smoking, annual influenza and pneumococcal vaccination, regular physical activity, inhaler technique review, long-term oxygen if chronically hypoxemic and pulmonary rehabilitation.

pucopd2.io: Outline appropriate patient education for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd2.q: When should varenicline be started relative to the quit date?
opts: On the quit date itself
Varenicline is not started on the quit date; it begins one week before it and continues for 12 weeks.
wrong stage or severity
One week after the quit date
Starting after quitting reverses the timing; varenicline begins one week before the quit date and continues for 12 weeks.
reversed direction or value
One week before the quit date
Correct. Varenicline is started one week before the quit date and continued for 12 weeks.
Once withdrawal symptoms begin
Varenicline is not started in response to withdrawal; it begins one week before the quit date and continues for 12 weeks.
wrong stage or severity

pucopd2.io: Discuss potential drug-drug, drug-food, and drug-herb interactions with drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd2.q: In which patient should bupropion be avoided rather than used with caution?
opts: One taking a tricyclic antidepressant
Tricyclic antidepressants, like venlafaxine, are noradrenergic antidepressants that call for caution with bupropion; avoidance is for monoamine oxidase inhibitors.
wrong stage or severity
One with cardiovascular disease
Cardiovascular problems are the caution for nicotine replacement (tachyarrhythmias, hypertension); bupropion is avoided with monoamine oxidase inhibitors and seizure disorders.
adjacent fact
One taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor
Correct. Bupropion is avoided in patients taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors and in seizure disorders; noradrenergic antidepressants (tricyclics and venlafaxine) call only for caution.
One with a history of depression
Depression and suicidal ideation are the neuropsychiatric events in varenicline's black box warning; bupropion is avoided with monoamine oxidase inhibitors and seizure disorders.
adjacent fact

pucopd2.io: Identify indications for drugs used for pulmonary infections, asthma, and COPD/COLD
pucopd2.q: Which feature of the inflammation in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease distinguishes it from asthma?
opts: It causes widespread reversible narrowing
Widespread reversible narrowing of the bronchial airways characterizes asthma; the inflammation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is generally not fully reversible.
competing diagnosis
It is generally not fully reversible
Correct. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is chronic inflammation of the airways and lung parenchyma that is generally not fully reversible, with an accelerated decline in lung function.
It is eosinophilic in the bronchial mucosa
Eosinophilic inflammation of the bronchial mucosa is how asthma is characterized; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is inflammation that is generally not fully reversible.
competing diagnosis
It spares the lung parenchyma
The inflammation involves the airways and the lung parenchyma; what sets chronic obstructive pulmonary disease apart is that it is generally not fully reversible.
reversed direction or value
